claims.text: Applying a silicide coating to a refractory high-entropy alloy promotes formation of a continuous protective silicide/oxide layer.
The protective layer produced by the silicide coating significantly reduces oxygen ingress and high-temperature oxidation.
MoNbTaTiW is an example of a refractory high-entropy alloy.
Refractory high-entropy alloys generally have poor native oxidation resistance.
The relevant substrate may be used in either an as-cast or homogenized state.
A Si-20Cr-20Fe silicide coating can be deposited by a fused-slurry method.
The coating is expected to provide protection over approximately 800–1200 °C in air or another oxygen-rich atmosphere for exposures of 10–100 hours.
High-temperature reaction between the coating and substrate produces a well-adherent, continuous scale containing MSi2 and/or a silica-rich phase.
The continuous silicide/oxide scale acts as a diffusion barrier to oxygen.
Slower oxygen diffusion into the bulk alloy minimizes further oxidation.
Suppressing oxidation preserves the alloy's microstructure and mechanical integrity.
The coated sample will show at least about a 50% reduction in oxidation mass gain relative to an uncoated sample under the same exposure.
The coated sample will retain superior mechanical properties relative to the uncoated sample after high-temperature oxidation.
Untreated refractory high-entropy alloys experience high-temperature oxidation that impedes their engineering use.
Oxidation of untreated refractory high-entropy alloys causes degradation of mechanical properties.
The benefit depends on the coating being uniform, adherent, and stable over the selected temperature and exposure time.
Thermal cycling stresses or mechanical damage may compromise the coating's effectiveness.
A controlled comparison at 800 °C in air for 10 hours can test oxidation mass gain, scale structure, and retained mechanical properties of coated and uncoated samples.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome specifies an approximately 50% or greater reduction in mass gain, whereas the falsification rule only requires a statistically significant decrease. A reduction smaller than 50% could therefore fail the quantitative prediction while not falsifying the hypothesis under the stated rule.
